en: The *Prameyaratnāvalī* composed by Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa:
Dependence upon the Blessed Lord.
Victorious is the illustrious Govinda, the Lord of the Gopīs, who sports with the cowherds; by his grace, I shall set forth this subtle *Prameyaratnāvalī*. 1.

May our devotion be eternally fixed upon that Reality, which is the Lord of Dharma whose name brings liberation to the universe, who is the very nature of eternal bliss and non-dual consciousness, and who finds satisfaction even with the mere semblance of devotion. 2.
May the ascetic named Ānandatīrtha, whose abode consists of bliss, be victorious—he whom wise people here proclaim to be the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. (3)
The lineage of gurus is always to be contemplated by the wise as being free from defects; through it, single-minded devotion is perfected, and by means of it, the delight of Hari arises. ||4||

As it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Those mantras which are devoid of a tradition (sampradāya) are considered fruitless. Therefore, in the Kali age, there will arise four lineage-holders: Śrī Brahmā, Rudra, Sanaka, and the Vaiṣṇava Kṣitipāvana; these four shall appear in the Kali age from Puruṣottama in Utkala. (Ka)
Śrī accepted Rāmānuja as her own; Caturmukha [Brahmā] accepted Madhvācārya; Rudra accepted Śrī Viṣṇusvāmin; and Catuḥsana [Viṣṇu] accepted Nimbāditya. (Kha)

In this regard, our own lineage of gurus is as follows: we praise in succession Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Brahmadevarṣi, Bādarāyaṇa; Śrī Mādhva, Śrī Padmanābha, and Śrīman Nara-hari-Mādhava; Akṣobhya, Jayatīrtha, Jñānasindhu, and Dayānidhi; Śrī Vidyānidhi, Rājendra, and Jayadharma; and then Puruṣottama, Brahmaṇya, and Vyāsatīrtha. Thereafter, with devotion, [we praise] Lakṣmīpati, Mādhavendra, and his disciples—Śrīśvara, Advaita, and Nityānanda—the teachers of the world.
We worship the divine Śrī Caitanya, the disciple of Īśvara, by whom the world was delivered through the bestowing of love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||ga||

Now the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are set forth: Śrī Madhva declared Viṣṇu to be the Supreme, known through all the scriptures, and that the universe, its reality, and the distinction between souls are true; he taught the gradation among those who resort to the feet of Hari, liberation as the attainment of Viṣṇu’s feet, pure devotion to Him as the cause thereof, and the three means of valid cognition—perception and so forth—as the authority for this. Thus does Lord Hari, the moon of Kṛṣṇacaitanya, instruct. (5)

The supreme nature of that Śrī Viṣṇu is as stated in the Śrī Gopāla Upaniṣad: "Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme deity; one should meditate upon him, taste him, worship him, and sacrifice to him."

And in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "Having known God, there is the casting off of all bonds; with afflictions destroyed, there is the abandonment of birth and death. Through meditation upon Him, upon the dissolution of the body, one attains the third state: universal sovereignty, absolute, with all desires fulfilled. And: "This is to be known as eternally established in the Self; indeed, there is nothing further to be known beyond this. And in the venerable Gītā: "There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya; all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread."
Because He is the cause, the substratum of qualities such as all-pervading consciousness and bliss, and because He possesses eternal Lakṣmī and other attributes, Kṛṣṇa is considered the supreme.

In this regard, its being the cause of all is as the Śvetāśvataras have said: "He who shines, illuminating all directions—above, below, and across—is like a fire; He is the one God, the Blessed One, the most excellent, who alone presides over the natures of the sources.
And: "The Source of the universe ripens His own nature and transforms all things that are to be ripened."
The state of being all-pervasive consciousness and bliss is as stated in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Having realized the great, all-pervasive Self, the wise man does not grieve."

The fact that consciousness has the nature of bliss is indicated by the word "Self" (ātman); for those who know this [explain] that from this [word], the state of being attainable by the liberated is understood. (7)
And the Vājasaneyins say: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss; it is the gift, the supreme goal of the giver."
And in the Śrīgopāla Upaniṣad:
"That one Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss..."

Embodiment must be understood as belonging to Citsukha alone who possesses desire; this is because of the mention of him as a "mass of consciousness" (vijñānaghana) and so forth. Furthermore, by this very [statement], it is demonstrated that there is no distinction between the body and the embodied one. || 8 ||
The omnipresence of that which possesses form is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"Like a tree, one stands firm in heaven; by that Puruṣa all this is pervaded."

Although residing in heaven, He is all-pervading; thus, by virtue of being described as having a form, the Lord is omnipresent. Furthermore, because He is directly perceived simultaneously by multitudes of meditators, He is of such a nature [as possessing a form].

And in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Tenth Canto: "He who has neither interior nor exterior, neither before nor after, who is both the world and that which is within and without the world—having considered that unmanifest Adhokṣaja, who bears a mortal form, to be his own son, the cowherd woman bound him with a rope to the mortar as if he were an ordinary being."
And in the Śrī Gītā: "By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded; all beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them. And yet beings do not abide in Me; behold My divine yoga."
The Lord possesses infinite power, which is expressed by the word "yoga"; it is the opinion of those who know reality that this [power] is what resolves all contradictions. (10)
By such [statements], his omniscience is established, as in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."
And in the Taittirīyaka [Upaniṣad], bliss is mentioned: "The knower of Brahman as bliss fears nothing from anywhere."

And [the qualities of] lordship, friendliness, the state of being a giver of knowledge, and the state of being a liberator are mentioned in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "The Lord of all, the Ruler of all, the refuge of all, the friend of all."
And from that, the ancient wisdom has issued forth.
It is the cause of bondage and the stability of liberation from saṃsāra.
And sweetness is described in the Śrīgopālopaniṣad:

"The Lord has eyes like beautiful lotuses, the luster of a rain cloud, and garments of lightning; he is two-armed, enriched with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and wears a garland of forest flowers."

The attributes are not distinct from the substratum, for their manifestation as distinct occurs only through qualification; since even for the learned there is the cognition that "time exists at all times," and so forth. (11)

Thus it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "His form consists of faultless, perfect qualities; He is self-dependent and devoid of the qualities of an insentient body. His hands, feet, face, belly, and other limbs consist solely of bliss; and His nature is everywhere free from internal differentiation."
Now, regarding her state of possessing eternal fortune, as stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"She, the Mother of the World, the Śrī of Viṣṇu, is indeed eternal and inseparable; O best of the twice-born, just as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, so too is she."
"Viṣṇu has three powers; among them, that which is proclaimed as the Supreme (Parā) is Śrī herself, who is non-different from Him—thus the Great Lord spoke to his disciples. (12)
In that regard, Viṣṇu possesses three powers, as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold; it is innate, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action."
The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas.

And in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "The supreme power of Viṣṇu is said to be one; likewise, another is called the individual soul (kṣetrajña); and a third power is recognized, known as ignorance and karma."
It has been stated in that very same place that Śrī is none other than Viṣṇu:

"May that Hari be gracious to us, whose power does not come within the range of the thread of time consisting of *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, *nimeṣas*, and so forth, even though he is pure. May that Viṣṇu, who is called the Supreme Lord and who, though pure, is [so addressed] by way of metaphorical designation, and who is the Self of all embodied beings, be gracious to us."
It is also stated in that very same place:

"In You, the sole refuge of all, there is but one [nature]—the *hlādinī*, the *sandhinī*, and the *saṃvit*. But in You, who are devoid of the *guṇas*, there is no mixed nature that causes both pleasure and pain."
Viṣṇu is one, and Lakṣmī is also one, yet she is ever inseparable from him; through her many self-perfected forms, she is designated as manifold.
In that regard, even while Viṣṇu is one, there is multiplicity, as stated in the Śrīgopāla Upaniṣad:

"Kṛṣṇa is the one controller, all-pervading and worthy of praise; though being one, he appears in many forms. Those wise ones who worship him seated upon his throne attain eternal happiness, and no others."
Now, regarding Lakṣmī, it is as follows: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold."
Although that fulfillment is universal and without distinction, nevertheless, there exists a gradation caused by the manifestation or non-manifestation of its power.
In that regard, Viṣṇu’s omnipresence is [declared] in the Vājasaneyaka:
"That is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises. Having taken the fullness of the full, only the full remains."
And in the Mahāvārāha [Purāṇa]:

"All the bodies of that Supreme Self are eternal and everlasting; they are devoid of loss or acquisition, and are never born of *prakṛti*. They are an abundance of supreme bliss, consisting of pure knowledge in every respect; all are complete with all virtues and entirely free from all defects."
Now, regarding Śrī, as it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:

"Just as Janārdana, the Lord of the Universe and God of gods, takes an incarnation, so too does Śrī act as his companion. Furthermore, when Hari was born from the lotus as the Sun, she became the Earth; and when he was Rāma Bhārgava, she became this very [Earth]. In his state as Rāghava she became Sītā, and at the birth of Kṛṣṇa she became Rukmiṇī; in other incarnations of Viṣṇu, she is his companion. In the state of a god she possesses a divine body, and in the state of a man she possesses a human form; indeed, she assumes a body that corresponds to the body of Viṣṇu."
It may be that fulfillment exists here in its own right due to identity; such is the opinion of those who hold the suffix -vin. || 15 ||

Nevertheless, there is still a gradation: in that regard, concerning Śrī Viṣṇu, it is as stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam—"These are portions and parts of the Supreme Person (puruṣa), but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself."
"And it is said that Hari himself was indeed the eighth among those two. Thus [it is stated].

Now, regarding Śrī, as stated in the *Atharva-upaniṣad* known as the *Puruṣabodhinī*: beginning with "In the district of Mathurā, in the place called Gokula," and mentioning that on two sides are Candrāvalī and Rādhikā, it further states that within her portion reside powers such as Lakṣmī and Durgā.
And in the Gautamīya Tantra:
"The goddess Rādhikā, the supreme deity, is said to consist of the nature of Kṛṣṇa; she consists of all Lakṣmīs, is all-beauty, and is the supreme enchantress."
Now, by the word "etcetera," its nature as the eternal abode is indicated, as in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "In what, O Venerable Sir, is it established? "In its own majesty."
"For this Self is established in the divine city of Brahman, in the midst of the ether," so it is said.
And in the *Ṛgveda*:
"We desire to go to those dwellings of yours where the many-horned, tireless cows are; for there, indeed, the supreme abode of the wide-striding Bull shines forth abundantly."
And in the Śrīgopālopaniṣad: "In the midst of them is indeed the city of Gopāla, which is Brahman itself."
And in the *Jitantastotra*:

"The world named Vaikuṇṭha, endowed with divine sixfold attributes, unattainable by non-Vaiṣṇavas, devoid of the three *guṇas*, crowded with eternally perfected beings who are absorbed in Him and perform the five-fold ritual (*pañcakālika*), joined with assembly halls and palaces, auspicious with groves and gardens, beautifully adorned with ponds, wells, lakes, and clusters of trees, non-material (*aprākṛta*), worshipped by the gods, and possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns. Thus it is said.
And in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*:
"The great abode called Gokula is a thousand-petaled lotus; its pericarp is that splendorous realm, born from an infinite portion of Him. Thus it is said.

Having brought the world, which is of His own nature, into manifestation within the phenomenal realm (prapañca), the Great Lord (Maheśvara) appears therein; this is the doctrine established by such terms as "Brahmā" and so forth. Just as the state of being a human child is attributed to Govinda—who is existence, consciousness, and bliss—by the ignorant, so too is the state of being material (prākṛtatā) falsely attributed to the Abode.
Furthermore, there is the state of eternal play (*nityalīlatva*); for thus says the Śruti: "That which has been, that which is becoming, and that which will be."
The one God, eternally devoted to His divine play, pervading all devotees, is the inner self within the hearts of His devotees.
And the Smṛti says:
"O Arjuna, he who knows in truth thus my divine birth and action, upon casting off the body, does not undergo rebirth; he comes to Me."

"Because of the infinity of form, the infinity of people, and the infinity of abodes, that karma is eternal; and because of its non-differentiation from them, so it has been declared by the best among the knowers of reality. (18)
Thus ends the first subject matter, titled "The Section on Dependence upon the Blessed Lord," in the *Prameyaratnāvalī*. || 1 ||
Furthermore, regarding the fact that He is known through all the Vedas, as stated in the Śrīgopāla Upaniṣad: "He who is sung of by all the Vedas."
And in the Kaṭhaka [Upaniṣad]: "That state which all the Vedas declare, and which all austerities proclaim."
And in the *Śrī Harivaṃśa*: "In the Veda, in the Rāmāyaṇa, in the Purāṇas, and likewise in the Mahābhārata—Hari is sung everywhere, at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end."
All the Vedas sing of Mādhava, both directly and through tradition; indeed, the Vedāntas sing of him directly, while others do so through tradition.

The fact that invarious places in the Vedas an inexpressibility is observed may be understood there as meaning that [the subject] cannot be expressed in its entirety; otherwise, it is my view that the undertaking of such [a work] would be futile.

Because of the absence of universals (jāti) and other such grounds for the application of words, the wise say that Brahman, being devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka), cannot be denoted by words at all. (3) But if it were inexpressible by any words whatsoever, there could be no indication (lakṣaṇā); and thus, it is my view that Brahman, being devoid of attributes, would not even be something indicated (lakṣya). (4)
Thus ends the second object of knowledge, titled "The Section on Being Knowable through All the Scriptures," in the *Prameyaratnāvalī*. 2.

"Viṣṇu, having created the entire world through his own power, made it appear real according to its nature"—since this has been said, this [statement] is indeed true; however, it is an untrue word intended for the purpose of generating dispassion. (1)
For thus it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"He who, being one and colorless, by the application of manifold powers, bestows many colors for the sake of established purposes."
And in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so too is this entire universe the power of the Supreme Brahman."
In the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad:

"He has pervaded all, the radiant, bodiless, woundless, without sinews, pure, untouched by evil; the seer, the wise one, the encompasser, the self-existent, who has ordained all things according to their true nature throughout eternal years. Thus it is said.
And in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"O best of sages, this entire world is thus imperishable and eternal, yet it possesses the conceptual variations of manifestation and disappearance, and birth and destruction."
And in the Mahābhārata: "Brahman is truth, austerity is truth, and Prajāpati himself is truth; from truth all beings are born; truth is this world consisting of the elements."

In passages such as "The Self, verily, this [was] in the beginning," those who know the Vedas have stated that the existence of the universe should be understood as being like a bird hidden in a forest. || 2 ||
Thus ends the third section of the *Prameyaratnāvalī*, titled "The Reality of the Universe. 3.
Now, regarding the reality of difference— that is, the difference of individual souls from Viṣṇu—
thus indeed do the Śvetāśvataras recite:
Two birds, companions and friends, cling to the same tree. Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating.
On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by a sense of powerlessness; but when he perceives the other, the Lord who is beloved, and His glory, he is freed from sorrow.

"Commencement, conclusion, repetition, novelty, fruit, eulogy, and corroboration—these six are said by the wise to be the marks for determining the purport [of a text]. These are perceived in the case of difference; therefore, that [difference] is its [the means of knowledge's] province. (1)
Furthermore, in the *Muṇḍaka*:

"When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person who is the source of Brahman, then the wise man, having shaken off both merit and sin, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality."
And in the Kaṭhaka: "As pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it, even so, O Gautama, does the self of the sage who possesses true knowledge become."
And in the Śrī Gītā:
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature; even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer."

Since a distinction is stated even regarding liberation among these [categories], the distinction must be ultimately real. [The opponent might argue: "I am Brahman, the one; I am the individual soul (jīva); there are no other souls, nor is there a Lord (īśvara). They exist only as imagined by my own ignorance (avidyā). But this is thus refuted, for otherwise the meaning of such scriptural passages as "He is eternal" and so forth would not be tenable.
For thus the Kaṭhas recite:

"The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who ordains the desires of the many—those wise ones who perceive Him abiding within themselves attain eternal peace, and no others."

From a single, eternal, and conscious Lord, many individual souls (jīvas) are distinguished by their mutual differences; therefore, this distinction is eternal. Just as speech and the other organs are termed "prāṇa" because their function depends solely upon the vital breath (prāṇa), so too the world is called "Brahman" because its existence depends upon Brahman.
For thus it is recited in the Chāndogya:
"One does not call them 'speeches,' nor 'eyes,' nor 'ears,' nor 'minds'; one calls them simply 'the vital breath' (prāṇa), for the vital breath indeed becomes all these."
Because it is pervaded by Brahman, some consider the world to be Brahman.
As it is said in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O Lord, this host of deities who has come into your presence is indeed true, because you, O All-pervading One, are the creator of the world."
The two positions regarding the discernment of reflections which have been accepted by others—namely, that [the mind] is omnipresent and that it is not an object—have been refuted by the wise. (7)
Is non-duality said by you to be different from Brahman or non-different? In the first case, there is the consequence of duality; in the latter, it is merely proving what is already established. (8)
"False and devoid of qualities, because it is not an object of valid cognition, Brahman is certainly not to be accepted by the wise"—thus spoke those who propound the true nature of reality. (9)
Thus ends the fourth topic of knowledge, titled "The Chapter on the Reality of Difference," in the *Prameyaratnāvalī*. 4.
Now, regarding the servitude of living beings to the Blessed One,
the Śvetāśvataras indeed recite:
"We know Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme divinity among deities, the supreme master among masters, the adorable God, the Lord of the world, who stands beyond."
And from the *Smṛti*: "Brahmā, Śambhu, as well as Arka, Candramas, and Śatakratu—these and others likewise are indeed joined with the splendor of Viṣṇu," and so forth.
"Along with Brahmā, the Rudras, and Indra, the gods together with the great seers worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the foremost of the gods. Thus it is said.
And in the *Pādme Jīvalakṣaṇa*: "He is the servant of Hari alone, and never of anyone else."
Thus ends the fifth jewel of knowledge, titled "The Section on the Servitude of Living Entities to the Blessed Lord," in the *Prameyaratnāvalī*. 5.
Now, regarding the gradation of individual souls (jīvas):

even though there is equality among souls due to the lack of distinction in their nature as atomic consciousness, their state of being knowers, and so forth, a gradation nevertheless exists on account of their spiritual practices (sādhana). || 1 ||
In that regard, its atomicity is stated by the Śvetāśvataras:
"The individual soul (jīva) should be known as a part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold; yet it is capable of infinity."
The nature of consciousness and qualities such as being a knower are described in the *Ṣaṭpraśnopaniṣad*:
"For he is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the perceiver, the agent—the person whose essence is consciousness (*vijñānātman*)."
And by the quality of pervasiveness, there is the state of pervading the body; as stated in the Śrī Gītā:
"Just as the one sun illumines this entire world, so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire field."
And the author of the Sūtras has indeed said: "Or [the soul's movement] is due to its qualities, as in the case of light."
The eternity of the qualities has been stated by the Vājasaneyins: "Verily, O Maitreyī, this Self is indestructible and its nature is imperishable."

Thus, although there is equality [in their nature], the wise declare that inequality regarding this world is clearly due to past actions (karma), whereas that pertaining to the next world is due to the various degrees of devotion (bhakti).
For thus the Kauthumas recite:
And there is a traditional teaching (smṛti): "Whatever kind of contemplation one has, such will be one's accomplishment."

The five states beginning with tranquility (śānti) and ending with passion (rati) have been proclaimed; among men who meditate upon the Lord by means of these, a gradation of degrees is recognized. (3)
Thus ends the sixth subject of inquiry, titled "The Section on the Gradations of Living Beings," in the *Prameyaratnāvalī*. 6.
Liberation consists in the attainment of Kṛṣṇa; now, regarding the fact that the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is liberation:
as in "Having known the God, there is the casting off of all bonds," and so forth; and also "The one controller, the all-pervading Kṛṣṇa, the one to be praised," and so forth.
The Lord Kṛṣṇa himself shines in many ways through manifold forms; having worshipped him, the liberated ones dwell happily in his eternal state. || 1 ||
Thus ends the seventh jewel of knowledge, titled "The Chapter on Liberation in the Form of Attaining Kṛṣṇa," in the *Prameyaratnāvalī*. 7.
The bestowal of liberation through pure devotion, and the causality of absolute devotion for emancipation,
as stated in the Śrī Gopālatāpanī Upaniṣad:
The vessel of the mendicant is this very mental construction directed toward that [Supreme] through the absence of conditions pertaining to this world or the next; this alone is *naiṣkarmya*.
And in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"Service to Hṛṣīkeśa by means of the senses, when it is free from all limiting adjuncts and rendered pure through being directed toward Him, is called devotion (*bhakti*)."
And this [devotion] is ninefold, as stated in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*:

"Hearing, chanting, remembering, serving the feet, worshiping, bowing down, servitude, friendship, and self-surrender—when devotion characterized by these nine marks is truly offered by a person to Viṣṇu, the Blessed One, I consider that to be the highest learning."
If service to the virtuous and service to the guru are performed with the same disposition as toward a deity, then this devotion to the Blessed One is attained; it is never obtained otherwise.
Service to the virtuous through the divine attitude is as stated in the Taittirīyaka: "Be one for whom the guest is a god."
Devotion to Him [arises] through that [association], as it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:

"The minds of these [people] do not touch the feet of the One of Wide Strides—that for which the removal of all misfortune is sought—as long as they do not choose the sprinkling of the dust from the feet of the Great Ones, who possess nothing."
Service to the teacher with the attitude toward a deity is as stated in the Taittirīyaka: "Be one for whom the teacher is a god."
And in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"For that great-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as for the Divine, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth."
Devotion to Him [is attained] through that [service], as stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata:

"Therefore, one who desires to know the supreme good should take refuge in a guru who is deeply learned in the revealed scripture (śabda) and the supreme reality (para), and who is a refuge of tranquility. There, regarding the guru as one's own self and deity, one should learn the duties of a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata-dharma). Through sincere and constant service to him, Hari—who is both the Self and the giver of the Self—becomes pleased."
Having obtained the five purificatory rites and attained the two kinds of devotion, he realizes Hari directly and rejoices eternally in His abode.
In this regard, there are five purificatory rites (saṃskāras) as stated in the Smṛti:
branding with heat, the sectarian mark (puṇḍra), the name, the mantra, and sacrifice as the fifth. Indeed, these five purificatory rites are the causes for supreme single-minded devotion.

In this context, "tapaḥ" (asceticism) refers to the wearing of marks such as the heated discus and other symbols; by that very term, the wearing of the name of Hari and other such marks is also implied. (3)
As it is stated in the Smṛti: "One should mark one's body with the syllables of Hari's name using sandalwood paste and the like; having become a purifier of the world, he shall attain his world."

The *puṇḍra* is the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), which is recorded in the scriptures as being of many kinds; it takes the form of the temple of Hari or His feet and brings about great auspiciousness. Its name is declared by the virtuous to be indicative of one’s status as a servant of Hari. The mantra consists of eighteen syllables or more, and is considered to be the very form of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*). The worship of the Śālagrāma stone and other such objects is designated by the term *yāga*. The authorities for these matters are to be seen by the virtuous in the Purāṇas and other texts. (4)
Devotion is ninefold, preceded by ritual injunction and inclination; through this twofold devotion, Kṛṣṇa himself becomes pleased and grants whatever desired abode [one seeks].

The God, assuming forms such as the four-armed one, is worshipped according to the prescribed rule; by means of that [worship] consisting of aesthetic delight (ruci), he is fully adored in human form.

One should perform the worship of Tulasī, Aśvattha, Dhātrī, and other deities, and remain steadfast in one's abode. A day of Hari (Ekādaśī) that is pierced by the dawn (aruṇodaya) must be abandoned; likewise, one should avoid a Janmāṣṭamī and similar observances that are pierced by sunrise.
Seeking the welfare of the world, the wise man, firmly established in his practice, should perform both regular and occasional rites without abandoning devotion as the primary principle.
One should, with diligent effort, avoid the ten offenses against the Name.
In this context, exclusive devotion (ekāntabhakti), which has the attainment of Kṛṣṇa as its fruit, is described. Preceded by knowledge and dispassion, it shall manifest its fruit immediately.
Thus ends the eighth jewel of the subject matter, titled "The Chapter on How Pure Devotion Bestows Liberation," in the *Prameyaratnāvalī*. ॥८॥
There are three means of valid cognition;
that is, only perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition.
As it is stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam:
Revelation, direct perception, tradition, and inference constitute the fourfold means of knowledge.
Since tradition (aitihya) is included within direct perception (pratyakṣa), the Teacher declared that there are three means of valid cognition; among these, the Veda (śruti) is the primary one.
Perception and inference are pure by virtue of their association [with the Self], since perception is seen to be fallacious in cases such as the vision of a phantom head.
And inference [is seen] regarding a mountain with excessive smoke, or one whose fire has been extinguished by rain; therefore, that too is not accepted as an independent means of valid cognition. (3)
Reasoning that is consistent with the truth is considered valid, whereas dry reasoning is to be avoided.
For thus say the Vājasaneyins:
"Verily, my dear, the Self is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."
The Kāṭhakas [state]:
"This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning; it is to be taught by another for the sake of right knowledge, O dearest one."

And *smṛti* states: "Reasoning (*tarka*) is the investigation, such as 'What could be the intended meaning here that is not inconsistent with what precedes and follows?'; however, one should avoid fallacious reasoning (*śuṣkatarka*)."
Since the cognition of Brahman does not arise for those who do not know the Veda, and since Brahman is that which is known through the Upaniṣads, therefore the Śruti is considered primary.
For thus says the Śruti: "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One. "I ask about the Person of the Upaniṣads."
Thus ends the ninth object of knowledge, titled "The Section on the Threefold Nature of the Means of Valid Cognition," in the *Prameyaratnāvalī*. 9.
Thus it was stated by the predecessor:

"In the illustrious Madhva school, Hari is the supreme; the world is real; in truth there is difference [between them]; the hosts of individual souls are attendants of Hari who have attained states of low and high; liberation is the experience of one's own innate bliss; pure devotion is the means to that; the triad beginning with perception is the authority; and Hari is the one object of knowledge for the entire Vedic tradition. (1)
In this work, there are nine jewels of valid cognition composed by Ānandatīrtha; this *Prameyaratnāvali* should be cherished in the heart with reverence by the wise. (2)
May Murāri, whose very self is consciousness, dwell eternally in our hearts—he upon whom the faultless and blissful Lord of Elephants looks with compassion. 3.
Thus ends the *Prameyaratnāvalī*, composed by the venerable Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa, the teacher of the tradition of the illustrious Lord Kṛṣṇacaitanya.
This work is complete.
